title: Savitri walks after Yama
hookLine: Savitri meets fate with effort, and a book on desire argues the same.
carry: fate is real, and effort is still the means
tomorrow: a king borrows his son's youth. was it worth it?

cards: In the Mahabharata, Princess Savitri chooses her own husband: Satyavan, son of a blind king living in exile in the forest. Then the sage Narada brings terrible news. Satyavan has one year to live.
Her father begs her to choose again. She won't. She marries him and counts the days.
Three days before the end she fasts. On the last day she follows Satyavan into the forest, and when Yama, lord of death, comes for his life, she walks after Yama.
She speaks with him so wisely that he grants her wish after wish, until one wish can only come true if Satyavan lives. Yama gives him back.

teach.b: Hindu thought has names for that struggle: daiva, fate, and purushakara, human effort. Savitri didn't deny the prophecy. She met it with everything she had: her vow, her fast, her feet on the road, her words.
Many married Hindu women still honor her in the Vat Savitri fast, praying and tying threads around a banyan tree for their husbands' long lives.
The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter takes up the same question with critics who say time and fate decide everything. Vatsyayana grants that luck is real.
Then his answer: success depends on human effort as its means. Even what's bound to happen comes about through some means. And a person who does nothing enjoys no happiness.
Ecclesiastes, in the Jewish and Christian Bibles, faces the same worry.

teach.h: A DESTINED SEED STILL NEEDS PLANTING.
teach.b: In the King James Version it admits that "time and chance happeneth to them all," and later answers: "In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand."
What they share: luck is real, and it isn't a reason to stop. And the honest difference. Ecclesiastes sets the not-knowing inside the work of God.
Vatsyayana argues from means and effort, and his chapter doesn't turn to God to make the case.

how: Hindu thought weighs fate (daiva) and human effort (purushakara) side by side, and many married Hindu women keep the Vat Savitri fast in Savitri's honor. Jews and Christians read Ecclesiastes on time, chance and sowing.

games.q: what does “the kama sutra's ethics chapter” mean?
o: the part of a well-known old book that says luck is just a myth
the part of a well-known old book that says fate decides it all
the part of a well-known old book that argues effort against fate

games.q: fate, effort, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: walked after Yama and won Satyavan back
time and chance happen to all

s: Vatsyayana says hard work always guarantees success
he grants that luck is real; he says effort is the means, and doing nothing brings no happiness.
he says a person who does nothing enjoys no happiness
his answer to the critics who leave everything to time and fate.
Ecclesiastes and the Kama Sutra make the same case, the same way
both say keep sowing; Ecclesiastes sets it within God's unseen work, Vatsyayana argues from means and effort.

games.q: a friend's new bakery has two slow months. she says the neighborhood's luck has turned, so she's shelving the new menu until it turns back. what do Vatsyayana and Ecclesiastes both suggest?
o: try several small things, since you can't know which will take.
wait it out. if luck turned, no effort will change it.
bet everything on one big idea; enough effort guarantees it.
games.why: Vatsyayana: effort is the means, even for what's bound to happen. Ecclesiastes: sow morning and evening, for you don't know which will prosper. neither promises a guarantee.

practice: Say quietly, once, one small thing you'll do toward something whose outcome you can't control: an application, a hard conversation, a seed in a pot. If you pray, offer the effort and leave the outcome with God.
If you don't, simply let it go. Then rest your hands open on your knees and breathe.

wordCard.voice: The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: the answer to fate. Effort is the means, and a person who does nothing enjoys no happiness.

orig.note: Sanskrit purushakara, human effort: the chapter's answer to those who leave it all to fate.

carryVoice: For the road: fate is real, and effort is still the means. Savitri walked after Yama. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Aranyaka (Vana) Parva (Savitri and Satyavan: Narada's prophecy, her fast, her following Yama and winning boons until Satyavan's life is returned)
Kama Sutra 1.2 (the objection that artha comes by fate and time; Vatsyayana's answer that success depends on human effort; one who does nothing enjoys no happiness)
